description: Making Health Promotion Meaningful: Community-engaged Strategies for Reaching Diverse Priority Populations Presented by Simona C. Kwon, DrPH, MPH Simona C. Kwon, DrPH, MPH, is an associate professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and serves as director of the NYU Center for the Study of Asian American Health. She is nationally recognized for her expertise in community-based participatory research (CBPR) and health equity initiatives aimed at reducing health disparities in immigrant and minority populations. Dr. Kwon’s research focuses on chronic disease prevention, cultural competency in healthcare, and the social determinants of health. She has led multiple NIH-funded projects addressing health issues in underserved communities, with a particular focus on Asian American populations. As a leader in public health, Dr. Kwon collaborates with community-based organizations to design and implement culturally tailored interventions. Her work highlights the importance of building trust and partnerships between healthcare systems and the communities they serve. She has published extensively on CBPR methodologies and health equity frameworks. Dr. Kwon is committed to advancing inclusive and equitable approaches to improving health outcomes across diverse populations. Learning Objectives: At the end of this activity, learners will be able to: Apply key principles of social marketing and cultural adaptation that can inform efforts to close gaps between current and ideal practice in health promotion and disease prevention for reaching priority populations. Describe how community engagement, participatory approaches, and cultural relevance can support more whole-person, integrated care through clinical practice, research, and education for diverse priority populations. Identify broad strategies for adapting evidence-based health programs to improve relevance, implementation, and sustainability in priority communities, with the goal of improving health outcomes. UCSF adheres to the ACCME’s Standards for Integrity and Independence in Accredited Continuing Education. Any individuals in a position to control the content of a CE activity, including content planners, reviewers, authors, presenters, moderators, panelists, or others are required to disclose all financial relationships with ineligible entities. All relevant financial relationships have been mitigated prior to the commencement of the activity. Accreditation: In support of improving patient care, the University of California, San Francisco Office of Continuing Medical Education (CME) is jointly accredited by the Accreditation Council for Continuing Medical Education (ACCME), the Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education (ACPE), and the American Nurses Credentialing Center (ANCC), to provide continuing education for the healthcare team. This CME activity meets the requirements under California Assembly 1195, continuing education, and cultural and linguistic competency. description: Exercise can improve physical functioning in cancer patients. It can reduce the feelings of fatigue, depression, nausea and weakness that can arise during and after cancer treatment. The UCSF Core and More class includes Pilates-based mat exercises to work on core strength and stability. We use rollers, bands and body weight as tools to enhance range of motion, flexibility, balance and muscular strength. Our goal is for you to have fun and increase your ability to perform daily activities. This class is sponsored by the UCSF Cancer Resource Center. It is open to current UCSF cancer patients and survivors. Registration is required for this class. To participate, you must undergo a pre-screening with an exercise counselor. For more information, call (415) 502-5547. There may be a waitlist for this course.

description: The UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center's Office of Community Engagement presents: CAB2: Chat & Chew Lecture Series Speaker: Mark Jesus Mendoza Magbanua, MS, PhD Laboratory Medicine Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center UC San Francisco Talk Title: Can a Blood Test Help Us Stay One Step Ahead of Breast Cancer? Understanding Liquid Biopsy and Its Potential to Improve Cancer Care About the Speaker: Dr. Magbanua is a Professional Researcher/Senior Scientist in the Department of Laboratory Medicine at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). He has extensive expertise in liquid biopsy, cancer genomics, and data science, with a particular focus on advancing precision oncology in breast cancer. He leads research projects investigating circulating tumor DNA (ctNA) in the I-SPY trial, an adaptive clinical trial evaluating neoadjuvant therapies for earty-stage breast cancer. His earlier research focused on developing technologies to detect and characterize circulating tumor cells (CTs), contributing to advances in liquid biopsy research. His work has provided important insights into the clinical significance and biological characteristics of tDNA and CTCs in breast cancer. As a principal investigator of NCI-funded R01 research grants, Dr. Magbanua focuses on integrating tDNA with imaging, molecular, and clinical biomarkers to improve the prediction of treatment response and ong-term outcomes in early-stage breast cancer. His research also explores innovative approaches for solating and characterizing tumor cells and analyzing cell-free DNA in malignant effusions from patients with metastatic breast cancer. His overarching goal is to develop and clinically validate liquid biopsy technologies that enable more precise treatment decisions and ultimately improve outcomes for cancer patients., powered by Localist, the Community Event Platform

description: The Academic Senate is pleased to announce the selection of Margot Kushel MD, as the recipient of the Fourth Annual Faculty Research Lectureship in Social, Behavioral, and Health Policy Sciences for her groundbreaking research on homelessness, housing instability, health, and the translation of evidence into policy and systems change. The lecture, titled “Housing, Homelessness, and Health: Bringing Evidence to the Policy Discussion.” will take place on Thursday, December 10, from 3:30pm – 5:00pm at Rock Hall, 1550 4th St., on Mission Bay Campus, with a small reception to follow. The lecture will also be broadcast on Zoom. Dr. Kushel is an internationally recognized leader in health services research whose work has advanced understanding of the causes and consequences of homelessness, the relationship between housing and health, and evidence-based approaches to preventing and ending homelessness. Her work combines rigorous research with community engagement and policy translation, with particular attention to older adults and other populations experiencing structural marginalization. Over the course of her career, she has authored nearly 200 peer-reviewed publications and has served as principal investigator or co-investigator on numerous federally funded studies. A defining feature of Dr. Kushel’s work is its direct connection to policy and practice. In 2019, she established the UCSF Benioff Homelessness and Housing Initiative (BHHI) with a $30 million gift from Marc and Lynne Benioff, bringing together researchers, people who experienced homelessness, policymakers, service providers, and community organizations to translate findings into action. She is also principal investigator of the California Statewide Study of People Experiencing Homelessness (CASPEH), the most comprehensive study of homelessness in California in decades. The study surveyed a representative sample of 3,200 adults across the state, and its findings have informed policymakers and helped reshape public understanding of homelessness and its potential solutions. Dr. Kushel has also led pioneering research on older adults experiencing homelessness through the National Institute on Aging-funded Health Outcomes of People Experiencing Homelessness in Older Middle Age (HOPE HOME) study. Since 2012, the study has generated important findings on functional decline, social isolation, health care utilization, mortality, and the “graying” of the homeless population, while informing legislation and national policy discussions. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Dr. Kushel helped develop and implement responses for people experiencing homelessness, including Project Roomkey, testing and vaccination efforts, and shelter-based public health protocols. Margot Kushel, MD, is Professor of Medicine and Division Chief of the Division of Health and Society in the UCSF Department of Medicine at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital and Trauma Center. She is Director of the UCSF Benioff Homelessness and Housing Initiative and the UCSF Action Research Center for Health. She also maintains an active internal medicine practice at the Richard Fine People’s Clinic at Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital, caring for patients with complex medical and social needs. The Fourth Annual Faculty Research Lecture in Social, Behavioral, and Health Policy Sciences will be held on Thursday, December 10, from 3:30pm – 5:00pm at Rock Hall, 1550 4th St., on Mission Bay Campus and will be broadcast on Zoom. The Faculty Research Lecture in Social, Behavioral, and Health Policy Sciences award was established in 2023. This award is bestowed on an individual member of the UCSF faculty with outstanding achievements in social, behavioral, and health policy research. UCSF faculty are asked to consider the outstanding research contributions of their colleagues and submit nominations for this prestigious award to the Academic Senate Committee on Research. The Committee on Research selects a recipient of this award annually., powered by Localist, the Community Event Platform
